paragraphs: Treating offline reinforcement learning as sequence prediction lets models learn patterns across recorded states and actions. However, a high-return sequence can reflect both good decisions and favorable events outside the agent’s control. The paper argues that modeling everything together makes it difficult to distinguish these contributions, encouraging overly optimistic decisions when environments are stochastic or adversarial.

The proposed method explicitly separates the policy model from the model of the world. This distinction lets the system reason separately about which actions it can choose and which environmental outcomes it may face. At test time, it searches for policies that remain robust across multiple possible futures, rather than relying on a favorable predicted continuation.

The authors demonstrate superior performance on several simulated autonomous-driving tasks. These findings support separating decision-making from environmental prediction when uncertainty matters. The evidence is specifically about performance in simulation; the central methodological contribution is a way to address optimism caused by confusing controllable actions with uncertain world dynamics.
icml-2022-addressing-optimism-bias-in-se.tldr: Separating policy and world models helps sequence-based reinforcement learning search for decisions that withstand multiple possible futures.

paragraphs: Skills let a reinforcement-learning agent act through extended behaviors instead of choosing every low-level action independently. Discovering these behaviors from expert trajectories can support more complex learning. Existing offline approaches, however, require users to choose the number of skills beforehand, creating a need for environmental knowledge or an additional search over that setting.

The paper first develops an offline method for learning options, a particular way of representing skills, using variational inference and continuous relaxations. It then connects skill discovery to Bayesian nonparametrics. The resulting model uses a carefully structured approximate posterior whose number of options can change dynamically, making inference tractable without fixing that number in advance.

The authors also show how the nonparametric extension can apply to other skill frameworks. Across several environments, their experiments demonstrate that the approach can outperform leading offline skill-learning algorithms. Its practical significance is that deciding how many behaviors to represent becomes part of learning, rather than a separate hyperparameter choice imposed before examining the trajectories.
icml-2022-bayesian-nonparametrics-for-of.tldr: A Bayesian nonparametric approach discovers skills from offline trajectories while allowing the number of skills to change during learning.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization chooses evaluations of an expensive black-box function using information from previous results. Many formulations assume that feedback arrives immediately or after a fixed delay. In applications such as hyperparameter tuning or clinical trials, evaluations can instead finish at unpredictable times, leaving the optimizer with incomplete feedback when another decision must be made.

This paper develops algorithms for that randomly delayed setting. The goal is to keep launching useful evaluations while earlier results remain pending, allowing parallel experimentation without requiring every outstanding evaluation to finish. The algorithms come with sublinear regret guarantees: their cumulative performance gap grows more slowly than the number of decisions under the analyzed setting.

The analysis also leads to contributions for batch Bayesian optimization and contextual Gaussian process bandits. Experiments on synthetic and real-life datasets support the algorithms’ performance. Together, the results address both the statistical choice of what to evaluate next and the practical timing problem created when feedback arrives asynchronously.
icml-2022-bayesian-optimization-under-st.tldr: The paper develops Bayesian optimization algorithms that keep selecting evaluations despite random feedback delays, with sublinear regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Center-based clustering can settle into poor local solutions. Recent variations of k-means address this through implicit annealing using generalized means, but their geometry is most suitable for roughly spherical clusters. This paper extends those algorithmic ideas to data whose generating mechanisms need a different notion of distance from a cluster center.

The method combines generalized-mean clustering with Bregman divergences. These divergences correspond to exponential-family distributions, providing a way to align clustering with a broader range of data types. Their mathematical structure also preserves closed-form updates, so the extension retains a simple computational form despite accommodating more varied distributions.

The authors establish finite-sample bounds that relax the bounded-support assumption used in prior work. Simulated experiments and a rainfall case study show improvements over peer methods in several non-Gaussian settings. The contribution therefore joins three concerns: avoiding poor local minima, choosing a suitable geometry for the data, and retaining an algorithm whose updates and theoretical behavior can be analyzed directly.
icml-2022-bregman-power-k-means-for-clus.tldr: Bregman power k-means extends annealing-based clustering to broader data distributions while retaining closed-form updates and finite-sample guarantees.

paragraphs: A learning-to-defer system decides whether to make a prediction itself or hand the decision to a human. This requires useful estimates of when the human will be correct. The paper studies calibration: whether the probabilities assigned to expert correctness have the meaning the system relies on when deciding to defer.

The authors identify a problem in an existing multiclass formulation. Its parameterization is not calibrated for expert correctness and does not even guarantee valid probabilities for that purpose. They propose a replacement based on one-vs-all classifiers that can produce calibrated estimates. Its loss also remains a consistent surrogate for the multiclass deferral objective, connecting the training criterion to the desired decision problem.

Experiments cover hate-speech detection, galaxy classification, and skin-lesion diagnosis. In these evaluations, calibration improves without sacrificing accuracy; accuracy is comparable to or often better than the earlier formulation. The result matters because reliable handoff decisions depend on meaningful confidence estimates as well as the overall correctness of the combined system.
icml-2022-calibrated-learning-to-defer-w.tldr: One-vs-all classifiers provide calibrated estimates of human correctness for learning to defer, without an observed accuracy cost in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering groups objects using pairwise evidence of similarity and dissimilarity. Its strongest approximation algorithms can depend on linear-programming relaxations that are too expensive for large instances. This paper targets two established versions of the problem, cluster editing and cluster deletion, with the aim of retaining useful solution quality while making computation more practical.

The key step connects these clustering problems to edge-labeling problems based on strong triadic closure. These connections yield more practical linear-programming approaches and highly scalable combinatorial methods that avoid the expensive relaxations. The latter include what the authors identify as the first combinatorial approximation algorithm for cluster deletion.

In practical evaluations, the resulting solutions nearly match the quality of the best algorithms while handling instances orders of magnitude larger. The finding is a trade-off improvement rather than a claim of exact optimization: the methods produce approximate clusterings, but make high-quality approximation accessible at substantially larger scales through a different formulation of the underlying problem.
icml-2022-correlation-clustering-via-str.tldr: Connections to strong triadic closure yield scalable approximation algorithms for cluster editing and deletion with near-leading empirical solution quality.

paragraphs: Federated learning often requires a server to average gradients computed by many clients. Sending those gradients can be expensive, so clients compress them before transmission. Because compression loses information, the server’s estimate of the average becomes less accurate. Different communication budgets and missing packets make this estimation problem harder.

EDEN is a distributed mean-estimation technique designed to handle both unequal communication budgets and packet loss. These conditions matter together because participating clients may differ substantially in how much information they can send and how reliably it arrives. A useful averaging method must accommodate that variation while controlling the inaccuracies introduced by communication constraints.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees for EDEN and evaluates it empirically. The reported results consistently improve on leading distributed mean-estimation techniques in the evaluations. The contribution concerns a central operation within federated learning: obtaining a useful aggregate from compressed, unevenly delivered client information. Improving that operation addresses a source of estimation error that can otherwise degrade the learning process.
icml-2022-eden-communication-efficient-a.tldr: EDEN improves distributed mean estimation while accommodating differing client communication budgets and packet loss.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a signal in generalized linear models whose design matrices are rotationally invariant. Such matrices can have arbitrary spectral distributions, allowing the model to express complex correlation structures. This broadens the setting beyond the Gaussian-design assumption used by an existing form of approximate message passing.

The authors introduce a family of approximate message-passing algorithms for this broader matrix class. They rigorously describe the algorithms’ performance in the high-dimensional limit through a state-evolution recursion, a sequence of equations tracking their behavior. The method has the same order of computational complexity as the Gaussian-design algorithm and includes that earlier algorithm as a special case.

Numerical experiments show performance close to Vector AMP while using much less computation, because the proposed method avoids an expensive singular value decomposition. Vector AMP is conjectured to be Bayes-optimal in some settings; proximity to its numerical performance does not establish that property for the new method. The stated benefit is broader correlation modeling with efficient computation and rigorous asymptotic characterization.
icml-2022-estimation-in-rotationally-inv.tldr: A new AMP family handles rotationally invariant designs with rigorous high-dimensional analysis and avoids the costly decomposition required by Vector AMP.

paragraphs: Regret measures the performance lost while learning compared with following an optimal policy. A first-order regret bound adapts to the optimal policy’s value on the particular problem, instead of relying only on worst-case quantities. Obtaining this kind of guarantee has been difficult in reinforcement learning with large state spaces.

The paper establishes such a bound in linear Markov decision processes. Its leading term scales with the square root of the optimal policy value multiplied by the number of episodes, alongside factors involving feature dimension and horizon. There is also an additive term depending on dimension, horizon, and the logarithm of the episode count.

To obtain the result, the authors develop a robust self-normalized concentration bound using Catoni’s mean estimator. They show that existing least-squares-based techniques are insufficient for this guarantee. The contribution therefore combines an instance-sensitive learning bound with a new statistical tool for controlling estimation error; the authors also suggest that this tool may be useful independently of the reinforcement-learning application.
icml-2022-first-order-regret-in-reinforc.tldr: Robust estimation enables regret bounds for linear MDPs that depend on the optimal policy’s value rather than only worst-case quantities.

paragraphs: In cooperative multi-agent learning, agents may choose their individually highest-valued actions while still failing to achieve the best team outcome. The paper traces this problem to restrictions in linear and monotonic decompositions of the joint action-value function. These representations can suffer from relative overgeneralization and fail to align individual greedy choices with optimal coordination.

The authors derive expressions for these joint value functions and use a transition diagram to identify possible convergence points. Their proposed greedy-based value representation changes this structure in two ways. Inferior target shaping makes the optimal node a self-transition node, while superior experience replay removes non-optimal self-transition nodes, leaving the desired coordination outcome as the target.

The guarantee is conditional: with true Q values and sufficient exploration, GVR ensures correspondence between individual greedy actions and optimal team performance. When true values are unavailable, the method instead achieves an adaptive balance between optimality and stability. Experiments across several benchmarks report improvements over leading baselines, complementing the theoretical account of when optimal coordination is ensured.
icml-2022-greedy-based-value-representat.tldr: GVR reshapes value learning to support optimal team coordination, with a guarantee requiring true Q values and sufficient exploration.

paragraphs: Kernel mean embeddings summarize probability distributions in a feature space, making them useful for comparing real and generated data. Their infinite-dimensional form is difficult to handle in differentially private generation. An earlier method, DP-MERF, uses finite random features, but the large number needed worsens the sensitivity of the resulting distribution summary.

This paper replaces random features with Hermite polynomial features. Their ordering provides the key advantage: lower-order features contain more distributional information than higher-order ones. Consequently, a relatively low-order collection can approximate the mean embedding more accurately than a much larger collection of random features, improving how compactly the distribution is represented.

The more informative representation helps improve the privacy–accuracy trade-off relative to DP-MERF. The authors demonstrate this on heterogeneous tabular datasets and image benchmarks. The contribution shows why feature selection matters for private generation: representation quality and sensitivity are connected, so an efficient summary can support better accuracy under privacy constraints without requiring an excessively large random-feature approximation.
icml-2022-hermite-polynomial-features-fo.tldr: Ordered Hermite polynomial features provide compact distribution summaries that improve the demonstrated privacy–accuracy trade-off in private data generation.

paragraphs: This paper examines how quickly classification error can decrease when a learning problem has more than two classes. Its central organizing idea is the margin condition, which describes how clearly the correct classification decision is separated from alternatives. The analysis asks how assumptions about that separation affect the error guarantees available to learning methods.

Under a hard-margin condition, the authors prove exponentially decreasing classification error for a wide variety of methods, without a bias–variance trade-off in the stated result. This is a conditional guarantee: the strong rate is tied to the margin assumption. Other margin assumptions lead to different convergence rates, making the structure of the classification problem central to the analysis.

The work extends results previously known for binary classification to the multiclass setting through a self-contained analysis. Its significance is that adding more possible labels does not, by itself, rule out very fast error decay. Suitable separation assumptions can still support strong guarantees, and the paper explains how those guarantees change with the assumed margins.
icml-2022-multiclass-learning-with-margi.tldr: Suitable hard-margin conditions yield exponential classification-error rates for many multiclass methods without a bias–variance trade-off.

paragraphs: Standard training need not update every neural-network parameter at the same frequency. This paper divides parameters into fast and slow groups, with the slow group updated less often. The aim is to reduce computation by assigning different update schedules to different parts of a network, especially during transfer learning.

With suitable parameter partitions, the authors show that vision and language models can be fine-tuned in almost half the time without reducing their resulting generalization performance. They also analyze convergence and compare the multirate scheme with ordinary stochastic gradient descent. These results connect the practical speed improvement to a study of the underlying optimization procedure.

The paper additionally considers how parameter splits might improve generalization when training from scratch. It discusses multirate updates as a way to learn different features and as a form of regularization. Those possibilities broaden the motivation beyond speed, while the concrete reported timing result concerns transfer-learning applications and depends on choosing appropriate partitions.
icml-2022-multirate-training-of-neural-n.tldr: Updating different parameter groups at different frequencies nearly halves fine-tuning time in reported applications without reducing generalization.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization has two sets of parameters, each associated with its own objective. It appears in hyperparameter optimization, meta-learning, and dataset distillation. When one level admits several equivalent optima, the objective alone does not determine which solution will be selected. The optimization procedure can therefore influence the result through an implicit preference.

The paper investigates these preferences in gradient-based methods that jointly optimize the two levels. It distinguishes cold-start and warm-start approaches and studies choices such as hypergradient approximation. The authors show that these decisions can substantially affect either the converged solution or the method’s long-run behavior, making them consequential parts of the optimization setup.

A further finding is that warm-start solutions can encode substantial information about the outer objective even when the outer variables have few dimensions. This highlights how the coupled optimization process can shape what a solution retains. The authors argue that understanding such implicit bias should play a central role in bilevel optimization, as it already does in single-level neural-network optimization.
icml-2022-on-implicit-bias-in-overparame.tldr: Bilevel optimization algorithms can select markedly different solutions through initialization practices and hypergradient approximations, even when objectives admit equivalent optima.

paragraphs: Nearest-prototype classifiers label an input according to its closest representative example, making their decisions interpretable. Robustness certification asks how much an adversary must change an input to alter that label. This paper examines cases where the distance used for classification differs from the distance used to measure an adversarial change.

The authors analyze combinations of the 1, 2, and infinity norms. For classifiers using Euclidean distance, they provide scalable algorithms that compute the minimum adversarial perturbation exactly; other cases receive improved lower bounds. They then use efficient lower bounds to train robust prototype classifiers, obtaining stronger Euclidean robustness guarantees than neural networks on MNIST.

The paper also reports what the authors believe are the first certification results for the LPIPS perceptual metric. On CIFAR10, their classifier’s certified robust accuracy exceeds the empirical robust accuracy reported in the cited comparison. These are distinct forms of evidence: certification establishes a guarantee, whereas empirical robustness describes measured performance under evaluation.
icml-2022-provably-adversarially-robust-.tldr: New exact computations and lower bounds strengthen robustness certification and training for interpretable nearest-prototype classifiers.

paragraphs: The paper develops a learning algorithm for stochastic shortest-path problems using linear function approximation. Its focus is the combination of statistical performance, computational efficiency, and policy structure. Rather than studying only how much regret can be bounded, it also asks whether the algorithm can be implemented efficiently and use stationary policies.

Under assumptions the authors characterize as minimal, the proposed algorithm achieves sublinear regret while satisfying both additional requirements. Sublinear regret means that the cumulative performance gap grows more slowly than the amount of interaction, so the average gap decreases. The authors identify this combination as the first of its kind in the linear-function-approximation literature, to their knowledge.

The efficient algorithm is also a special case of a broader method. With access to a computation oracle, that general method achieves regret proportional to the square root of the number of episodes. The oracle condition matters: the broader statistical guarantee and the directly computationally efficient construction are related results, but they carry different computational qualifications.
icml-2022-regret-bounds-for-stochastic-s.tldr: An efficient algorithm combines linear function approximation, stationary policies, and sublinear regret for stochastic shortest-path problems.

paragraphs: Retrosynthesis works backward from a desired product to the reactants that could produce it. The paper introduces Retroformer, a Transformer architecture for predicting those reactants. Its end-to-end, template-free approach performs molecule editing without relying on cheminformatics tools, placing that part of the prediction process within the learned architecture.

The central design is a local attention head that jointly encodes a molecule’s sequence and graph representations. It lets information move between the local region involved in a reaction and the broader reaction context. This connects a representation of molecular structure with the contextual information needed to reason about the overall transformation.

The authors report state-of-the-art accuracy for end-to-end template-free retrosynthesis and improved molecule and reaction validity relative to many strong baselines. They also describe the generation procedure as highly interpretable and controllable. The stated contribution combines predictive performance with a mechanism for integrating local chemistry-related structure and global context during generation, rather than treating the molecular sequence as an isolated representation.
icml-2022-retroformer-pushing-the-limits.tldr: Retroformer combines molecular sequences and graphs through local attention to improve end-to-end, template-free reactant prediction.

paragraphs: Reward-free reinforcement learning explores before the reward function is known, then must produce a near-optimal policy once a reward is revealed. In tabular problems, this requires more samples than exploring with the reward already available. The paper shows that the corresponding separation in dimensional dependence disappears for linear Markov decision processes.

The authors give a computationally efficient reward-free algorithm with sample complexity proportional to d squared times H to the fifth, divided by epsilon squared, up to logarithmic factors. A lower bound for reward-aware learning also has quadratic dependence on d. The dimension dependence therefore matches, although the stated bounds have different horizon dependence.

The algorithm uses a new exploration procedure that gathers samples in specified feature directions. Its sample complexity scales optimally with the relevant analogue of maximal state-visitation probability. The same procedure can produce well-conditioned covariates. The result identifies linear structure as a way to collect broadly useful exploratory data without paying the extra dimensional cost that reward-free learning incurs in tabular settings.
icml-2022-reward-free-rl-is-no-harder-th.tldr: In linear MDPs, efficient reward-free exploration achieves dimension dependence matching a reward-aware lower bound, despite differing horizon factors.

paragraphs: Accurately evaluating a policy depends on the data available about its decisions and outcomes. This paper studies how to collect that data efficiently and safely in bandit settings. It places the data-collection policy itself at the center of the problem, connecting exploration choices to the quality of later policy evaluation and comparison.

The authors formulate the problem and examine several representative variants. For each variant, they analyze statistical properties and derive a corresponding exploration policy. They also provide an efficient algorithm for computing that policy, linking the desired statistical behavior to a procedure that can actually choose how data should be gathered.

Both theoretical analysis and experiments support the usefulness of the methods. The contribution is a framework for treating evaluation data as something to design deliberately, with safety and efficiency considered together. Its emphasis on multiple variants also makes clear that the appropriate exploration policy depends on the particular evaluation problem being posed, rather than assuming one collection strategy fits every case.
icml-2022-safe-exploration-for-efficient.tldr: The paper formulates safe, efficient data collection for bandit policy evaluation and derives computable exploration policies for several variants.

paragraphs: Algorithmic reasoning research asks whether neural networks can learn to carry out procedures associated with classical algorithms. Individual studies often generate specialized data to test a particular hypothesis. That practice makes results difficult to compare across publications and creates additional work for researchers entering the field.

The CLRS benchmark provides a shared collection of tasks drawn from algorithms in Introduction to Algorithms. It spans sorting, searching, dynamic programming, graph processing, string processing, and geometry. This breadth gives researchers a common basis for studying learned algorithm execution across different kinds of procedures, instead of relying solely on isolated task-specific evaluations.

The authors run extensive experiments with several popular algorithmic-reasoning baselines and use their performance to highlight connections to open challenges. They also release a library for using the benchmark. The main contribution is a common evaluation resource: it helps organize evidence about what models can do across algorithm families and reduces the need for each study to construct its own evaluation setup.
icml-2022-the-clrs-algorithmic-reasoning.tldr: CLRS provides a shared benchmark spanning classical algorithms to make neural algorithmic-reasoning evaluations easier to compare.

paragraphs: Learning a model of an environment could help an agent adapt quickly when that environment changes. This paper tests whether prominent deep model-based reinforcement-learning methods deliver that potential. Using an improved Local Change Adaptation setup, the authors find that PlaNet and DreamerV2 adapt poorly to localized environmental changes.

Together with earlier observations about MuZero, these findings suggest a broader concern about current methods. The authors investigate elements that hinder adaptation and connect them to techniques commonly used in deep model-based learning. The study therefore examines why having a learned world model may fail to translate into effective behavioral adjustment.

They empirically test their insights under linear function approximation, showing that a modified linear Dyna method can adapt effectively to local changes. Experiments with nonlinear Dyna then explore the challenges of extending adaptive behavior to nonlinear models. The results distinguish the potential benefits of model-based learning from the adaptation abilities of particular implementations and identify concrete directions for investigating that gap.
icml-2022-towards-evaluating-adaptivity-.tldr: Local-change tests reveal adaptation weaknesses in prominent model-based RL methods and show effective adaptation with a modified linear Dyna method.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent must contend with noisy gradients and problem-specific quantities that affect useful step sizes. For smooth, strongly convex objectives, this paper shows that exponentially decreasing step sizes can adapt to unknown gradient-noise variance when smoothness is known. The resulting rate combines an exponentially decaying term with a noise term proportional to variance divided by the iteration count.

Adapting to unknown smoothness creates a separate challenge. The authors show that stochastic line search achieves the desired rate only to a neighborhood of the solution. An offline smoothness estimate instead permits convergence to the minimizer, with a slowdown proportional to the estimation error. These results separate noise adaptation from adaptation to the objective’s geometry.

Adding Nesterov acceleration improves the exponential term’s condition-number dependence from the condition number to its square root, while retaining noise adaptation. Offline estimates of smoothness and strong convexity still allow convergence, but more slowly. Experiments also support exponential step sizes combined with a new stochastic-line-search variant.
icml-2022-towards-noise-adaptive-problem.tldr: Exponential step sizes give SGD and accelerated SGD noise-adaptive rates, while adapting to unknown problem constants introduces distinct convergence trade-offs.

paragraphs: Attribution methods such as Shapley values assess how input components contribute to an output by evaluating partial inputs. For an ordinary classifier, however, it can be unclear what a partial input should mean. Common counterfactual constructions may fall outside the data distribution, making their evaluation difficult and susceptible to manipulation.

The paper proposes training neural networks directly as characteristic functions, which are designed to evaluate partial inputs. It does this through simple two-player games and applies the setup to Connect Four. During training, agents randomly lose access to color information, making partial observation an explicit part of the task they learn.

This construction reduces ambiguity about how missing information is represented and removes the need for off-distribution evaluations in the proposed comparison setup. It also allows explanation methods to be compared through game play against one another. The contribution is an evaluation setting where the model’s handling of partial information is trained directly, providing a concrete basis for studying attribution methods.
icml-2022-training-characteristic-functi.tldr: Training Connect Four agents with hidden color information creates characteristic functions that support direct, game-based comparisons of attribution methods.

paragraphs: Scene graphs represent objects as nodes and their relationships as edges. Generating realistic examples can support scene synthesis and training-data augmentation. The challenge differs from molecular graph generation: scene graphs contain much larger vocabularies of objects and relationships, and their semantic rules are implicit rather than defined by chemical structure.

VarScene addresses this with a variational autoencoder that treats a scene graph as a collection of star-shaped subgraphs. The encoder represents those component stars in a latent space. The decoder learns to sample stars and the edges connecting them, building a complete graph from these local components and their connections.

Training uses maximum mean discrepancy to compare the distribution of generated scene graphs with the ground-truth distribution. Experiments show that VarScene reproduces the underlying scene-graph generation process more accurately than several leading baselines. The stated result supports decomposing complex scene graphs into structured local pieces while learning how those pieces combine into realistic whole-graph configurations.
icml-2022-varscene-a-deep-generative-mod.tldr: VarScene generates scene graphs by learning latent representations of star-shaped components and how to connect them.

paragraphs: Neural-network loss landscapes are difficult to visualize, so researchers often inspect a straight path between two parameter settings, such as initialization and the trained model. A smooth path or a barrier can seem informative about optimization difficulty. This paper tests whether those visual patterns justify broader conclusions about training success.

The authors systematically change the data, initialization, optimizer choices, and architecture, then examine both linear-interpolation behavior and final performance. They also apply interpolation to individual layers and network substructures. This lets them investigate whether the visual behavior of the whole network reflects more specific sensitivities within its components.

They find that some layers are particularly sensitive to initialization, but the shape of the linear path does not indicate the corresponding changes in test accuracy. The results cast doubt on treating the presence or absence of interpolation barriers as a necessary indicator of optimization success. Linear slices can reveal behavior along the chosen path, while the study challenges broader performance inferences drawn from that picture.
icml-2022-what-can-linear-interpolation-.tldr: Linear loss-landscape slices reveal initialization sensitivities but do not reliably indicate changes in test accuracy in the reported study.
